title: SR-22 Insurance Explained: What It Is, How Long You Need It, What It Costs and the FR-44 Difference
description: SR-22 insurance explained: who needs one, the usual 3-year term, filing fees, non-owner SR-22s, and how Florida and Virginia's FR-44 differs.
author: Insurance Bhaiya Research Desk
keyTakeaways: An SR-22 is **not insurance**. It's a certificate your insurer files with the state to prove you carry at least the minimum liability cover.
Commonly required after a DUI, driving uninsured, serious violations or a licence suspension, usually for **about 3 years** (it varies by state).

The filing fee is usually modest (often around $15–$50). The real cost is the **high-risk premium** behind it (see [how much does car insurance go up after a DUI](/qa/how-much-does-car-insurance-go-up-after-a-dui)).
If your policy lapses, the insurer notifies the state (usually with an SR-26), which can lead to a **licence suspension** and restart the clock.
**Florida and Virginia** use the **FR-44**, which requires double the state minimum liability limits. In Florida that's 100/300/50.

faqs.question: Is SR-22 insurance a special type of policy?
faqs.answer: No. It's a certificate attached to a normal auto policy, proving to the state that you carry the required liability cover. See the [car insurance for high-risk and convicted drivers](/learn/car-insurance-for-high-risk-and-convicted-drivers) hub.

faqs.question: How long do I need an SR-22?
faqs.answer: Usually about 3 years from the date set by your state, but it varies by state and offence. A lapse can restart the period.

faqs.question: Can I get an SR-22 without a car?
faqs.answer: Yes, through a non-owner policy. See [what is a named non-owner car insurance policy](/qa/what-is-a-named-non-owner-car-insurance-policy).

content.text: If a court or DMV tells you to 'get SR-22 insurance', you're being told to prove to the state that you're insured, and to keep proving it for a set period. This guide is part of our [car insurance for high-risk and convicted drivers](/learn/car-insurance-for-high-risk-and-convicted-drivers) series. It explains how the filing works, what it costs and how to get through the requirement period without restarting it.

items: **DUI/DWI conviction:** the most common trigger. See [how much does car insurance go up after a DUI](/qa/how-much-does-car-insurance-go-up-after-a-dui).
**Driving without insurance**, or causing an accident while uninsured. See [what happens if you crash without insurance](/qa/what-happens-if-you-crash-without-insurance).
**Licence suspension or revocation**, including reinstatement after one. See [can you get auto insurance with a suspended license](/qa/can-you-get-auto-insurance-with-a-suspended-license).
**Serious or repeat violations**, such as reckless driving. See [how long does reckless driving affect insurance](/qa/how-long-does-reckless-driving-affect-insurance).
Buy a policy from an insurer that offers SR-22 filings in your state. Many standard carriers do, and [non-standard auto insurance](/glossary/non-standard-auto-insurance) carriers specialize in it.
The insurer files the SR-22 electronically with your state DMV and charges a filing fee.
Keep the policy continuously in force for the whole requirement period, usually about 3 years.
If the policy cancels or lapses, the insurer files an SR-26 (cancellation) and the DMV can suspend your licence.
When the period ends, confirm with the DMV that the requirement has been lifted before you change or drop cover.

content.title: One Missed Payment Can Restart Your Clock
content.text: A lapse of even a few days can trigger suspension, and in many states it resets the requirement period. Set up automatic payments, and read [what happens when insurance expires](/learn/what-happens-when-insurance-expires) and [can you pause car insurance](/qa/can-you-pause-car-insurance) before you change anything.

content.text: Florida drivers should also understand the state's base requirements in [do you need bodily injury insurance in Florida](/qa/do-you-need-bodily-injury-insurance-in-florida). The higher limits an FR-44 forces are often closer to what you *should* carry anyway. See [coverage vs limits](/learn/coverage-vs-limits) and the [California auto coverage scenario](/scenarios/jordan-california-auto-coverage).
No Car? Use a Non-Owner SR-22

If you need an SR-22 to reinstate your licence but don't own a vehicle, a [named non-owner car insurance policy](/qa/what-is-a-named-non-owner-car-insurance-policy) with an SR-22 attached is usually the cheapest way to comply. It covers your liability when you drive borrowed cars. If no insurer will write you at all, your state's [assigned risk auto insurance plan](/qa/what-is-an-assigned-risk-auto-insurance-plan) must offer cover.
UK Readers: Is There an SR-22 Equivalent?

No. UK insurers don't file certificates with the DVLA. Instead, the conviction itself is the issue, and you must declare it while it's unspent. See [how long do motoring convictions stay on your licence](/qa/how-long-do-motoring-convictions-stay-on-your-licence), [do you have to declare spent convictions](/qa/do-you-have-to-declare-spent-convictions-for-car-insurance) and [which insurance companies do not ask about criminal convictions](/qa/which-insurance-companies-do-not-ask-about-criminal-convictions). Buying a repaired write-off with a conviction? Read [are Cat N cars more expensive to insure](/qa/are-cat-n-cars-more-expensive-to-insure), [Cat S vs Cat N](/compare/cat-s-vs-cat-n-car-insurance) and [Ryan's DR10 and Cat N scenario](/scenarios/ryan-leeds-dr10-cat-n-car-insurance).

Other high-risk routes: drivers with felony records should read [car insurance with a felony](/qa/can-you-get-car-insurance-with-a-felony). If you're declined everywhere, see [can an insurance company refuse to insure you](/qa/can-an-insurance-company-refuse-to-insure-you). Telematics can help rebuild your record during the SR-22 period (see [black box insurance for high-risk drivers](/qa/does-black-box-insurance-help-high-risk-drivers)). UK readers caught driving uninsured face an [IN10 conviction](/qa/what-is-an-in10-conviction) rather than an SR-22.
